title: Evaluating AI Output
description: A practical framework for reviewing AI responses before using them — so you catch problems before they cause trouble.

data.text: The skill of evaluating AI output is as important as the skill of prompting. A good habit here protects you from the biggest risks of AI use — and takes only seconds once you build the reflex.

Most AI-related mistakes do not happen because the model is broken — they happen because the output was used without review. The model produced something plausible, it went straight into a document or email, and the error only surfaced later. Evaluation is the step between generation and use. It does not have to be slow, but it does have to happen.
The SIFT review framework

SIFT is a four-step mental checklist for reviewing any AI response before using it. The four dimensions — Specific facts, Internal consistency, Fit for purpose, and Tone — cover the most common ways AI output goes wrong. Running through them takes under a minute once the habit is established.

terms.definition: Check any specific names, numbers, dates, or citations. These are where AI most often gets things wrong.
Does the response contradict itself? Does the conclusion follow from the reasoning it presented?
Does this actually answer the question you asked? Is the format right? Is the length appropriate?
Is the tone right for your audience? Does the AI have unintended slant or framing you should correct?

data.text: S — Specific facts: what to look for

The S step is the most important and most time-consuming. Specific facts are the outputs most prone to hallucination — and the ones most likely to damage your credibility if wrong. The category includes: statistics and percentages, proper nouns (names of people, companies, products), dates and years, URLs and DOIs, legal or regulatory citations, and any quoted text attributed to a real person.

A quick heuristic: the more specific and narrow a claim, the higher the hallucination risk. 'AI is widely used in healthcare' is broad and hard to get wrong. 'A 2022 McKinsey report found that 67% of healthcare executives planned to increase AI investment by 2025' is extremely specific — every element of it could be fabricated, partially correct, or subtly distorted. Verify those second-type claims against the named original source before using them.

Verify role, title, and affiliation are currently accurate
Find the original source; paraphrases often drift from the original

data.text: I — Internal consistency: spotting self-contradiction

Language models generate token by token and do not maintain a global view of what they have already written. This means a long response can contradict itself — recommending approach A in paragraph two and approach B in paragraph five, or citing one figure early on and a different figure for the same metric later. Internal consistency checks are especially important for: long-form reports, structured comparisons, numerical analyses, and multi-step reasoning.

When you catch a contradiction, the fix is usually simple: paste the two contradictory passages back to the model and ask it to reconcile them. A well-prompted follow-up like 'You said X earlier and Y here — which is correct, and why?' often produces a reliable correction. If the model cannot resolve the contradiction, that is a signal the topic is at the edge of its reliable knowledge.
F — Fit for purpose: did it answer the real question?

AI models sometimes answer a close-but-different version of the question asked. This is especially common when the prompt is ambiguous, long, or multi-part. The model may address the easiest or most salient interpretation rather than the one you intended. The Fit step asks: does this response actually give me what I needed? Common mismatches include: answering a general question when a specific one was asked, addressing the wrong audience level (too technical / too basic), producing the wrong format (a list when you needed prose), or covering only part of a multi-part question.

The fix is almost always in the prompt. If an output is off-target, identify precisely which part of your intent the model missed and add a clarifying instruction. 'You answered the general question, but I specifically needed X for audience Y in format Z' — regenerate with that addition and the output typically improves substantially.
T — Tone and bias: invisible framing

AI models inherit biases, associations, and stylistic tendencies from their training data. These surface as tone problems (too formal, too casual, too hedged, too confident), framing problems (presenting one perspective as neutral when it is not), and word-choice problems (using in-group vocabulary that excludes part of your audience). None of these are obvious errors — they require the human author's judgment about what the specific audience needs.

Common tone issues to watch for: AI frequently defaults to an overly optimistic or marketing-adjacent register when writing about technology or business topics. It often adds unnecessary hedging ('It's important to note that...', 'Of course...') that reads as filler. It may write in American English conventions by default when British or Australian conventions are needed. And it sometimes adopts an academic register when plain language is more appropriate. The T step is where your voice as a human author reasserts itself.
Matching verification effort to stakes

Not every AI output deserves the same scrutiny. A brainstorm list for an internal meeting has very different stakes from a published report or a client-facing document. Calibrating your verification effort to the actual risk prevents both under-checking (missing important errors) and over-checking (wasting time on low-stakes work where AI errors are harmless).

rows: Quick read through for obvious errors
Read and edit carefully; check any claims
Verify all specific facts against primary sources
Never rely on AI alone — consult qualified professional

data.text: Practical verification tools
Verification does not have to mean slow manual research. The right tool for the right claim type makes fact-checking fast enough to become a routine step rather than a special effort.

rows: Google Scholar (scholar.google.com), Semantic Scholar, DOI resolver (doi.org)
Search '[organization name] + [report title] + [year]' to find the original document
Whether a URL exists and says what was claimed
Click it; use web.archive.org if the page is no longer live
Wikipedia with source footnotes; Encyclopaedia Britannica
PubMed (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov), NHS or CDC official pages
Westlaw, LexisNexis, official government legislative databases
Perplexity AI (cites sources inline), browsing-enabled ChatGPT or Claude

data.text: Using AI to check AI: helpful but limited

You can ask an AI model to review its own output or to check another model's output — and this sometimes catches errors, particularly logical inconsistencies or poorly reasoned arguments. However, it has a structural limit: if the model does not know a fact, it cannot reliably check whether its own claim about that fact is correct. Two wrong outputs from the same model will often agree with each other.

Useful AI self-checks include: asking the model to identify claims it is uncertain about ('List any specific facts in the above that you are not confident are accurate'), asking it to check internal logic ('Does the conclusion in the last paragraph follow from the analysis in paragraphs 2 and 3?'), and asking it to steelman the opposite view ('What are the strongest objections to the argument above?'). These add value — but they are supplements to, not substitutes for, verification against real sources.

data.caption: AI self-checking is useful for logic and consistency but cannot reliably verify factual accuracy it does not know.

data.title: SIFT in action: evaluating a business email draft
data.content:
AI-drafted email says: "As per the Q3 results showing a 23% YoY growth, we should..."

S: Is the 23% YoY figure accurate? → Check with your actual data.
I: Does the recommendation logically follow from that growth rate? → Read through carefully.
F: Does this address the specific conversation thread the client had? → Make sure it matches context.
T: Is the tone appropriately professional without being stiff? → Adjust as needed.

This 30-second check prevents the embarrassment of sending wrong data to a client.

data.title: SIFT in action: evaluating a research summary
data.content:
AI-written summary says: "A 2021 MIT study found that 78% of remote workers reported lower productivity."

S: Does this study exist? Search Google Scholar for 'MIT remote work productivity 2021'. If you cannot find it, the citation is likely fabricated.
I: Does the rest of the summary consistently frame remote work negatively, or does it present multiple findings? A one-sided summary may be missing contrary evidence.
F: Did you ask for a balanced overview or a critique? Check that the summary matches your actual request.
T: Is this framed neutrally, or does it read like an argument against remote work? Adjust framing to match your document's purpose.

Specific institutional names (MIT, Harvard, WHO) paired with specific statistics are a high-risk hallucination pattern. Always verify before using in a published document.

data.text: Building the evaluation habit

The biggest barrier to good AI evaluation is not knowledge — it is the friction of pausing between generation and use. The output looks finished. It sounds confident. The temptation to copy-paste immediately is strong. Building the SIFT habit means creating a deliberate pause: before the output goes anywhere, run through the four letters. Even a 20-second scan is better than none.

A practical workflow: after getting an AI response, do not highlight-and-copy immediately. Instead, read it once for comprehension, then ask yourself the SIFT questions. For high-stakes outputs, open a second tab for verification as you read rather than planning to verify 'later' — later rarely happens once the output is in a document.

You do not need to verify everything. For creative writing or brainstorming, verification is rarely needed. For factual claims in formal documents, public communications, or high-stakes decisions — always verify.
Your domain expertise is the first filter

No verification tool replaces subject-matter knowledge. An experienced accountant reading an AI-generated tax explanation will immediately notice a wrong assumption that a general reader would miss entirely. A nurse reading an AI-generated clinical summary will catch a medication contraindication that looks correct in the output's confident prose. Your professional knowledge is active while you read — trust it.

This creates an important asymmetry in how you should think about AI assistance. In domains where you have expertise, AI errors are relatively easy to catch because you know what good looks like. In domains where you lack expertise — asking AI to draft legal language, interpret financial regulations, or explain a medical treatment you are unfamiliar with — you lose your most powerful error-detection tool. High-stakes use in unfamiliar domains is where professional verification is most critical and where AI errors are hardest to catch.
